introduction-the-memory-wall.core: Exact answers to 'have we seen this?', 'how many distinct?' or 'how often?' over billions of items need memory proportional to the data. Probabilistic data structures trade a small, bounded error for tiny, fixed memory and fast operations, which is ideal for streams, caches and analytics at scale.

first_principles.problem: Counting unique visitors exactly across 10 billion events needs hundreds of gigabytes of RAM.

analogy.title: Estimating crowd size from a photo sample
analogy.story: Count a sample area and multiply; you're close enough without counting every person.
analogy.breaks: Crowd estimates can be biased; these structures have mathematically proven error bounds.

example.title: Memory comparison
flow: Exact set of 1B user IDs: ~16 GB+

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Six orders of magnitude less memory.

check.q: What do probabilistic data structures trade for memory savings?
check.a: A small, bounded probability of error in their answers.

the-magic-sauce-hash-functions.core: Probabilistic structures rely on fast, well-distributed non-cryptographic hash functions (MurmurHash3, xxHash, CityHash) that map inputs to uniform-looking bits. Multiple independent hashes can be derived cheaply from two (Kirsch–Mitzenmacher double hashing: h_i = h1 + i·h2). Poor hashes skew results and break error guarantees.

first_principles.problem: A homemade hash clusters values and the Bloom filter's false-positive rate is ten times the target.
truths: Cryptographic hashes are slower than needed.
derivation: Seed hashes to avoid **adversarial** inputs when exposed.

analogy.title: Shuffling a deck thoroughly
analogy.story: A good shuffle spreads cards evenly; a lazy one leaves clumps that ruin the game.
analogy.breaks: Cards can be reshuffled; hash outputs are deterministic for the same input and seed.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: k positions for the cost of two hashes.

code.text:
import mmh3
def hashes(key, k, m):
    h1 = mmh3.hash(key, 0) & 0xffffffff
    h2 = mmh3.hash(key, 1) & 0xffffffff
    return [(h1 + i * h2) % m for i in range(k)]

check.q: Why not use SHA-256 for Bloom filters?
check.a: It's much slower than needed; fast non-cryptographic hashes give sufficient uniformity.

bloom-filters-the-membership-question.core: A Bloom filter is a bit array of m bits with k hash functions. Insert sets k bits; a query checks them: if any is 0, the item is definitely absent; if all are 1, it's probably present. There are no false negatives and a tunable false-positive rate (~1% at ~9.6 bits per item). Standard Bloom filters can't delete.

first_principles.problem: A database does expensive disk lookups for keys that don't exist.

analogy.title: A bouncer's list of first initials
analogy.story: If your initial isn't on it, you're definitely not invited; if it is, check the full list.
analogy.breaks: Initial lists are human-readable; Bloom bits are shared by many items, so you can't remove one safely.

example.title: LSM-tree lookups
flow: Each SSTable has a Bloom filter
Get(key): skip SSTables whose filter says 'no'
99% of disk reads for missing keys avoided

check.q: Can a Bloom filter return a false negative?
check.a: No; it can only return false positives.

cuckoo-filters-a-better-bloom-filter.core: Cuckoo filters store short fingerprints of items in buckets chosen by two hash locations (partial-key cuckoo hashing), relocating existing fingerprints when buckets fill. They support deletion, offer better space efficiency than Bloom filters at low false-positive rates and give faster lookups (two bucket reads), but insertions can fail when the table is near full.

first_principles.problem: A cache-membership filter needs deletes when items are evicted, which Bloom filters can't do.
derivation: Two buckets: **i1 = h(x), i2 = i1 ⊕ h(fp)**.

analogy.title: A cuckoo chick pushing others out of the nest
analogy.story: New entries displace old ones to their alternative nests until everyone fits.
analogy.breaks: Cuckoo chicks are ruthless; filters give up after a bounded number of kicks.

example.title: Bloom vs Cuckoo
flow: Dynamic cache membership with evictions → Cuckoo

check.q: What key capability do cuckoo filters add over Bloom filters?

hyperloglog-the-how-many-uniques-questio.core: HyperLogLog estimates distinct counts by hashing items and tracking, in m registers, the maximum number of leading zeros seen (a rare long run implies many items). Combining registers with a harmonic mean gives ~1.04/√m standard error, about 0.8% with 16,384 registers in 12 KB. HLLs merge by register-wise max, so they work across shards and time windows.

first_principles.problem: Daily unique users must be computed across 50 shards and combined into weekly totals.
truths: Long runs of zeros are rare.
derivation: Hash item; **first p bits** pick a register.
Store **max leading zeros** of the rest.

analogy.title: Guessing how many coins were flipped from the longest run of heads
analogy.story: A run of 20 heads suggests about a million flips.
analogy.breaks: One coin run is very noisy; HLL averages thousands of registers to reduce error.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Weekly uniques from daily sketches, 12 KB each.

PFADD visitors:2026-10-18 user:1 user:2 user:3
PFCOUNT visitors:2026-10-18
PFMERGE visitors:week visitors:2026-10-12 visitors:2026-10-13 ... visitors:2026-10-18
PFCOUNT visitors:week

check.q: Why can HyperLogLogs from different shards be merged?
check.a: Each register stores a maximum, and the max of maxima equals the max over the union.

count-min-sketch-the-how-often-question.core: A Count-Min Sketch is a d×w matrix of counters with d hash functions. Each increment adds to one counter per row; a query takes the minimum across rows. Collisions only inflate counts, so estimates never undercount, with error ≤ εN (ε = e/w) with probability 1 − δ (δ = e^−d). It's used for heavy hitters, rate limiting and frequency analytics.

first_principles.problem: Tracking request counts per IP for millions of IPs exactly needs too much memory.
truths: Taking the minimum reduces collision error.

analogy.title: Several tally sheets with shared lines
analogy.story: Each sheet groups some names together; the smallest tally across sheets is closest to the truth.
analogy.breaks: Tally sheets can be audited; sketches can't list which items they counted.

check.q: Can a Count-Min Sketch underestimate an item's count?
check.a: No; collisions only add, so it can only overestimate.

combining-structures-the-top-k-pattern.core: Finding the top-k most frequent items in a stream combines a Count-Min Sketch (approximate counts for any item) with a min-heap of size k holding current candidates. On each item, update the sketch, read its estimate and replace the heap's minimum if the estimate is larger. Space-Saving and Misra-Gries are alternatives with deterministic guarantees.

first_principles.problem: A CDN wants the top 100 most requested URLs per minute across billions of requests.
truths: Only candidates near the top matter.
derivation: On update: if estimate > heap min, **replace**.

analogy.title: A leaderboard fed by an approximate scorekeeper
analogy.story: The scorekeeper estimates everyone's score; only those beating the bottom of the board get listed.
analogy.breaks: Leaderboards are exact; sketch estimates can promote an item slightly wrongly.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Top-100 URLs maintained in KBs of memory.

check.q: What two structures combine to find top-k in a stream?
check.a: A Count-Min Sketch for counts and a min-heap of size k for candidates.
